{{Short description|Description of phase separation}}
The '''Cahn–Hilliard equation''' (after [[John W. Cahn]] and [[John E. Hilliard]])<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Cahn|first1=John W.|last2=Hilliard|first2=John E.|date=February 1958|title=Free Energy of a Nonuniform System. I. Interfacial Free Energy|url=http://aip.scitation.org/doi/10.1063/1.1744102|journal=The Journal of Chemical Physics|language=en|volume=28|issue=2|pages=258–267|doi=10.1063/1.1744102|bibcode=1958JChPh..28..258C |issn=0021-9606|url-access=subscription}}</ref> is an [[equation]] of [[mathematical physics]] which describes the process of [[Phase (matter)|phase]] separation, [[spinodal decomposition]], by which the two [[Component (thermodynamics)|components]] of a binary [[fluid]] spontaneously separate and form domains pure in each component. If <math>c</math> is the concentration of the fluid, with <math>c=\pm1</math> indicating both domains, then the equation is written as<math display="block">\frac{\partial c}{\partial t} = D\nabla^2\left(c^3-c-\gamma\nabla^2 c\right),</math>where <math>D</math> is a [[diffusion]] coefficient with units of <math>\rm{L}^2/\rm{T}</math>, <math>\sqrt{\gamma}</math> gives the length of the transition regions between the domains, <math>\partial/{\partial t}</math> is the partial [[time derivative]] and <math>\nabla^2</math> is the [[Laplacian]] in <math>n</math> dimensions (typically three). Additionally, the quantity <math>\mu \equiv c^3-c-\gamma\nabla^2 c</math> is sometimes identified as a [[chemical potential]].

It is related to the [[Allen–Cahn equation]], as well as the stochastic Allen–Cahn and the stochastic Cahn–Hilliard equations.

==Features and applications==

Of interest to mathematicians is the existence of a unique solution of the Cahn–Hilliard equation, given by smooth initial data. The proof relies essentially on the existence of a [[Lyapunov function]]al. Specifically, if we identify

:<math>F[c]=\int d^n x \left[\frac{1}{4}\left(c^2-1\right)^2+\frac{\gamma}{2}\left|\nabla c\right|^2\right],</math>

as a free energy functional, then

:<math>\frac{d F}{dt} = -\int d^n x \left|\nabla\mu\right|^2,</math>

so that the free energy does not grow in time. This also indicates segregation into domains is the [[asymptotic]] outcome of the evolution of this equation.

In real experiments, the segregation of an initially mixed binary fluid into domains is observed. The segregation is characterized by the following facts.
[[File:CahnHilliard g0.5.gif|thumb|320x320px|Evolution of random initial data under the Cahn–Hilliard equation with <math>\gamma=0.5</math> and <math>C=0</math> (equal amounts of each phase), demonstrating phase separation.]]
* There is a transition layer between the segregated domains, with a profile given by the function <math>c(x) = \tanh\left(\frac{x}{\sqrt{2\gamma}}\right),</math> and hence a typical width <math>\sqrt{\gamma}</math> because this function is an equilibrium solution of the Cahn–Hilliard equation.
* Of interest also is the fact that the segregated domains grow in time as a [[power law]]. That is, if <math>L(t)</math> is a typical domain size, then <math>L(t)\propto t^{1/3}</math>. This is the Lifshitz–Slyozov law, and has been proved rigorously for the Cahn–Hilliard equation and observed in numerical simulations and real experiments on binary fluids.
* The Cahn–Hilliard equation has the form of a [[conservation law]], <math>\frac{\partial c}{\partial t} = -\nabla \cdot \mathbf{j}(x),</math> with <math>\mathbf{j}(x)=-D\nabla \mu</math>. Thus the phase separation process conserves the total concentration <math>C=\int d^n x c\left(x,t\right)</math>, so that <math>\frac{dC}{dt}=0</math>.
* [[File:CahnHilliard OstwaldRipening.gif|thumb|320x320px|Evolution of random initial data with <math>\gamma=0.5</math> and <math>C=-0.2</math> (60/40 mix of the blue and red phases, respectively), demonstrating [[Ostwald ripening]]]]When one phase is significantly more abundant, the Cahn–Hilliard equation can show the phenomenon known as [[Ostwald ripening]], where the minority phase forms spherical droplets, and the smaller droplets are absorbed through diffusion into the larger ones.

The Cahn–Hilliard equation finds applications in diverse fields: in complex fluids and soft matter (interfacial fluid flow, polymer science and in industrial applications). The solution of the Cahn–Hilliard equation for a binary mixture demonstrated to coincide well with the solution of a [[Stefan problem]] and the model of Thomas and Windle.<ref>{{cite journal |first1=F. J. |last1=Vermolen |first2=M. G. |last2=Gharasoo |first3=P. L. J. |last3=Zitha |first4=J. |last4=Bruining |year=2009 |title=Numerical Solutions of Some Diffuse Interface Problems: The Cahn–Hilliard Equation and the Model of Thomas and Windle |journal=International Journal for Multiscale Computational Engineering |volume=7 |issue=6 |pages=523&ndash;543 |doi=10.1615/IntJMultCompEng.v7.i6.40 }}</ref> Of interest to researchers at present is the coupling of the phase separation of the Cahn–Hilliard equation to the [[Navier–Stokes equations]] of fluid flow.
